npc-needs.advantage: Semantic descriptions could extend behavior in utility-AI / smart-object scenarios.
npc-needs.limitation: Need weighting, conflicts and long-term consistency are unspecified; traditional rules may be simpler and cheaper.
npc-needs.reported_result: The author shows a game prototype built with Claude and driven by Jev decisions.
npc-needs.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
npc-needs.plain_explanation: Give Jev a character's needs and available options, then execute its choice in the game. The model decides what to do; movement, animation and rules remain in game code.
npc-needs.review_summary: The needs-to-tool selection mechanism is plausible and the author acknowledges existing rule-based alternatives. Improved behavior or long-term coherence has not been measured.

npc-500.title: 500 agents in a 3D environment
npc-500.summary: Run decisions for many virtual characters in one 3D world.
npc-500.mechanism: Agents request Jev decisions and the simulator executes them; scheduling and batching details are unknown.
npc-500.advantage: Focuses on population scale and throughput under simulation load.
npc-500.limitation: 35 calls/second is not 35 updates per second for every agent; per-agent update frequency is absent.
npc-500.reported_result: The author reports 500 agents, 500ms average latency and 35 API calls/second for an initial implementation.
npc-500.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
npc-500.plain_explanation: Send characters' questions to Jev and execute their choices in the simulation. An overall rate of 35 requests/second does not mean each of 500 characters updates 35 times/second.
npc-500.review_summary: 500 entities, 500ms request latency and 35 total calls/s do not establish every entity’s decision rate or remove latency as a bottleneck. Under one call per agent, a full sweep would take about 14.3s; batching is unspecified, so that calculation is conditional.

driving-toy.title: “FSD” driving simulation
driving-toy.summary: A small driving simulation that the author calls “rebuilding FSD.”
driving-toy.mechanism: Jev participates in virtual driving control; sensors, controllers and state representation are unknown.
driving-toy.advantage: A visual example of fast decisions inside a driving simulation.
driving-toy.limitation: Not a reproduction of Tesla FSD or a real-road validation; it establishes no road-safety or autonomous-driving capability.
driving-toy.reported_result: The author says the prototype took under an hour and shares an approximately two-minute video.
driving-toy.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
driving-toy.plain_explanation: Code and Jev jointly control the simulated car. Driving in this environment is far from demonstrating safe real-road operation or reproducing Tesla FSD.
driving-toy.review_summary: Rebuilding Tesla FSD is a materially broader claim than a toy driving demo. Real-world perception, road testing, reliability and a matched system comparison are not provided; the prototype need not be false for the headline to overstate it.

realtime-driving.title: Unpaused real-time driving
realtime-driving.summary: Keep the car moving while Jev thinks to test real-time simulated driving.
realtime-driving.mechanism: Continuously advancing simulator state → Jev → raw control inputs; physics does not pause during network waits.
realtime-driving.advantage: Explicitly exposes latency and stale-state constraints rather than pausing the simulation.
realtime-driving.limitation: Still a simulator, without coverage, crash-rate or long-duration stability data.
realtime-driving.reported_result: The author explicitly states that the simulator runs without pausing for the model.
realtime-driving.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
realtime-driving.plain_explanation: Pausing the simulator for every model call hides latency. Here it keeps moving, so the observed state may already be outdated when an answer arrives.
realtime-driving.review_summary: The author explicitly bounds the work to an unpaused driving simulator. Timing logs and broad reliability are missing, but the source does not claim validated physical autonomy.

drone-sim.title: Jev drone simulation
drone-sim.summary: Fly through simulated obstacles with Jev choosing tactics and code stabilizing the drone.
drone-sim.mechanism: Project README: local code converts camera depth/segmentation buffers to symbolic scenes → Jev judges maneuvers, risk and target loss → ordinary code executes; control and safety run independently at higher rates.
drone-sim.advantage: Publishes perception, tactical decision and flight-control layers, including a baseline and failure boundaries.
drone-sim.limitation: MuJoCo simulation, not a real flight. The main successful comparison is a single run; an earlier seed-matched test showed no advantage over the baseline.
drone-sim.reported_result: The author reports about 15 minutes of setup and $0.10 spent.
drone-sim.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
drone-sim.source_notes: **Repository cross-check (2026-09-18)**: The [pinned README](https://github.com/RomanSlack/jev-drone/blob/cbeb53ce4f17a06ea490ae43effcdad231143610/README.md) specifies MuJoCo, symbolic camera scenes and layered control. Jev does not receive images directly, and safety code can override its actions in the main setup. The author also discloses a single-run result, an earlier comparison with no advantage and an unreliable tunnel experiment. This is a documentation review, not a reproduction.
drone-sim.plain_explanation: Like a navigator working with a flight controller, code summarizes camera information, Jev chooses maneuvers, and faster control/safety loops constrain the actions.
drone-sim.review_summary: The pinned documentation separates symbolic perception, classical control, safety vetoes and Jev advice, and discloses failures. It supports a narrow simulated hybrid-system result, not physical deployment or general superiority.

unstable-government.title: Unstable Government town
unstable-government.summary: Introduce a law in a fictional town and watch residents react before a newspaper is generated.
unstable-government.mechanism: Claude creates reactions and set pieces → Jev chooses residents' responses → town simulation → next-day newspaper.
unstable-government.advantage: Separates narrative generation from character choices for interactive storytelling.
unstable-government.limitation: Fictional reactions cannot be used as predictions of policy effects in the real world.
unstable-government.reported_result: The author demonstrates a mixed-model town with 40 residents.
unstable-government.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
unstable-government.plain_explanation: Claude creates possible reactions and scenes, Jev chooses for each resident, and the simulation acts them out. This is interactive storytelling, not policy forecasting.
unstable-government.review_summary: A clearly fictional hybrid-model town demo. It provides no empirical policy forecast, but the author frames it as entertainment rather than validated social science.

synthetic-personas.title: 150 fictional user personas
synthetic-personas.summary: Ask fictional users about product interest to explore early ideas.
synthetic-personas.mechanism: 150 fictional people each receive 12 questions for structured Jev judgments.
synthetic-personas.advantage: A quick way to explore persona/product fit and draft interview questions.
synthetic-personas.limitation: Synthetic opinions are not actual user research or market-demand validation.
synthetic-personas.reported_result: The author reports about five seconds and ¥1.8 JPY, including cross-region network latency.
synthetic-personas.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
synthetic-personas.plain_explanation: Define personas, then ask Jev fixed questions in their context. These are simulated opinions, not responses from real interview participants.
synthetic-personas.review_summary: The source explicitly uses fictional personas and reports a single runtime/cost. This can illustrate synthetic responses, not real demand, willingness to pay or validated market research.

typegpu-realtime.title: TypeGPU real-time semantic effects
typegpu-realtime.summary: Let camera and microphone input influence lighting and visual effects.
typegpu-realtime.mechanism: Camera/microphone → Moonshine, YOLO26 and DepthART → Jev → lights, shadows and bloom; ruNNtime and TypeGPU share GPU resources.
typegpu-realtime.advantage: Separates local perception from semantic decisions for interactive media.
typegpu-realtime.limitation: Jev is only one part of the pipeline; end-to-end latency and component ablations are absent.
typegpu-realtime.reported_result: The author demonstrates three neural-network inference paths running alongside rendering.
typegpu-realtime.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
typegpu-realtime.plain_explanation: Local models process speech, objects and depth; Jev makes semantic judgments; rendering code changes effects. Jev is one decision stage, not the whole perception/rendering pipeline.
typegpu-realtime.review_summary: The post explicitly names local perception, rendering and Jev components, supporting a composed demo rather than direct audiovisual understanding by Jev. Full latency, implementation verification and component comparisons are missing.

ask-jev.title: Ask Jev
ask-jev.summary: Enter a question and see Jev's judgment instead of a long written answer.
ask-jev.mechanism: User input → Jev judgment → website result; the author mentions Convex integration.
ask-jev.advantage: A public entry point that makes judgment-style output tangible.
ask-jev.limitation: An interaction/entertainment example; arbitrary judgments should not be treated as reliable factual answers.
ask-jev.reported_result: The author shares the website and an approximately 26-second demo.
ask-jev.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
ask-jev.plain_explanation: The site takes input, asks Jev for a judgment and displays it. It illustrates decision-style interaction, not a guarantee that arbitrary judgments are factual.
ask-jev.review_summary: A website and video support a judgment interface, as the author describes. They do not establish reliable answers to arbitrary factual questions.

word-chat.title: Finite-vocabulary chat
word-chat.summary: Give Jev a common-word list and let it build a conversation one word at a time.
word-chat.mechanism: Existing text and a finite vocabulary → choose the next word → append → repeat.
word-chat.advantage: Shows how choice outputs can be composed into a generative interaction.
word-chat.limitation: The vocabulary limits expression; per-word decision costs and latency are not directly comparable with a text model.
word-chat.reported_result: The author demonstrates chat built from common English words and punctuation choices.
word-chat.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
word-chat.plain_explanation: Jev chooses the next word from a finite list; code appends it and asks again. The loop constructs the text, and the vocabulary limits what it can say.
word-chat.review_summary: The author explicitly discloses a small word vocabulary and a selection loop, a bounded mechanism compatible with the demo. It does not establish a general text-generation API or competitive quality and efficiency.

character-chat.title: 29-option character generation
character-chat.summary: Let Jev choose one letter or punctuation mark at a time to build text.
character-chat.mechanism: Evaluate a–z, space, comma and period → append the highest-probability character → feed the updated text back.
character-chat.advantage: An explicit control loop with more freedom than a fixed word list.
character-chat.limitation: Character-level loops require many calls and do not establish a native text-generation API.
character-chat.reported_result: The author describes 29 character candidates and shares an approximately 15-second demo.
character-chat.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
character-chat.plain_explanation: Each round asks 29 yes/no questions, picks the strongest character and appends it. Producing text this way does not establish an advantage over a dedicated text model.
character-chat.review_summary: The post specifies 29 yes/no character questions and appending the highest-probability result. The substantiated claim is an autoregressive selection loop, not training a new general-purpose language model.

pixel-drawing.title: Parallel pixel drawing
pixel-drawing.summary: Combine many pixel-level judgments to experiment with drawing through Jev.
pixel-drawing.mechanism: The author describes predicting pixels in parallel; resolution, color choices and question construction are not disclosed.
pixel-drawing.advantage: An exploratory way to combine classification outputs into a visual artifact.
pixel-drawing.limitation: Not a validated general image generator; quality, resolution and total cost are unknown.
pixel-drawing.reported_result: The author shares an approximately 11-second drawing demo.
pixel-drawing.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
pixel-drawing.plain_explanation: Think of deciding picture cells and assembling them in code. The author describes parallel pixel prediction but does not publish color choices, resolution or question construction.
pixel-drawing.review_summary: A small drawing demo is compatible with composing pixel judgments. Resolution, palette, prompts and total cost are undisclosed; general-purpose image-generation quality is unestablished.

riscv.title: RISC-jeV logic-gate experiment
riscv.summary: Use Jev for simple logic decisions and compose them into small computer instructions.
riscv.mechanism: Jev judges AND/OR-style operations → SERV instruction execution → arithmetic, bit operations and printing.
riscv.advantage: An explicit hierarchy illustrates how decisions can compose into computation.
riscv.limitation: A concept experiment, not a computational-efficiency advantage; deterministic code is more appropriate for logic gates.
riscv.reported_result: The author publishes a live demo and names the SERV implementation.
riscv.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
riscv.plain_explanation: Like building a machine from blocks, Jev supplies AND/OR-style decisions that SERV combines into instructions. This illustrates composition rather than efficient computation.
riscv.review_summary: The author explicitly describes logic-gate judgments composed through SERV, not a native Jev CPU. Integration correctness, stability and any advantage over deterministic computation remain unverified.

trading-bot.title: Monad / Kuru trading bot
trading-bot.summary: Let Jev choose buy or sell from price information and have code submit the order.
trading-bot.mechanism: Asset-pair prices → Jev buy/sell choice → Kuru order book on Monad.
trading-bot.advantage: A clear decision-to-execution path for studying event-driven systems.
trading-bot.limitation: No return, drawdown or risk-control evaluation; fast execution does not establish profitability. The demo is not investment advice.
trading-bot.reported_result: The author says it can execute trades in each roughly 300ms block and provides a demo URL.
trading-bot.media_note: Image or video attached to the source post; the preview does not verify all implementation or performance claims.
trading-bot.plain_explanation: The model chooses an action and code connects to the blockchain order book. Fast orders do not imply profitable trading; complete returns and risk records are absent.
trading-bot.review_summary: The decision-to-order architecture is plausible, but trades and sustained end-to-end latency are unverified. A 300ms block interval is not a measured complete decision/execution cycle, and no profitable strategy is established.

predictive-launcher.title: Intent-aware predictive launcher
predictive-launcher.summary: Find files without remembering names: type “the PDF I just downloaded” and rank relevant matches first.
predictive-launcher.plain_explanation: Like asking an assistant for the document you just downloaded: the app prepares candidates and context, Jev interprets the request, and the interface updates its ranking as you type. Indexing details are undisclosed.
predictive-launcher.mechanism: The author describes Jev interpreting a query while it is typed and the launcher updating its ranked matches. File indexing, context construction, request throttling and permission scope are undisclosed.
predictive-launcher.advantage: Explores contextual requests such as “just downloaded” beyond filename or alias matching; useful for selecting among file candidates.
predictive-launcher.limitation: The roughly 100ms figure is author-reported. No evaluation covers large file collections, duplicate names or ambiguous references. High model confidence does not guarantee a correct match.
predictive-launcher.reported_result: The author shares a 20-second launcher demo and reports roughly 100ms decisions per keystroke, ranking the newest downloaded PDF first.
predictive-launcher.media_note: The original 20-second demo video, with its source cover and direct video link.
predictive-launcher.review_summary: A specific intent-based file query is demonstrated. The reported ~100 ms lacks scale, timing boundaries and error cases; high model confidence is not perfect retrieval accuracy.

live-commerce-assistant.title: Live shopping assistant and avatar expressions
live-commerce-assistant.summary: Recommend products during a conversation and change a virtual shop assistant’s expression with the dialogue.
live-commerce-assistant.plain_explanation: Like a shop assistant listening and bringing over products: the conversation system talks, Jev contributes quick judgments, and the app updates recommendations and expressions. The author demonstrates two models together but does not disclose every interface.
live-commerce-assistant.mechanism: The author combines Jev and gpt-live-1 to update product recommendations during a conversation and change avatar expressions with its content. The exact speech, ranking and expression-mapping responsibilities are undisclosed.
live-commerce-assistant.advantage: Places recommendations inside a live conversation; closer to a customer-facing shopping experience than offline intent labeling.
live-commerce-assistant.limitation: A simple demo without recommendation-relevance, inventory-consistency or end-to-end latency evaluation. Expression mapping does not establish a capability exclusive to Jev.
live-commerce-assistant.reported_result: The author shares a roughly 65-second live shopping demo using Jev and gpt-live-1, describing the expression feature as a simple implementation.
live-commerce-assistant.media_note: The main post’s roughly 65-second video; demonstration footage does not establish recommendation quality or conversion gains.
live-commerce-assistant.review_summary: The author identifies a simple demo using Jev plus gpt-live-1. End-to-end behavior is not solely attributable to Jev, expression mapping is not proven unique to it, and recommendation/inventory accuracy is unmeasured.

minecraft-hybrid.title: Minecraft with Jev, Astra and local policies
minecraft-hybrid.summary: Split Minecraft play across models: long-term planning, quick reactions, and local movement and aiming.
minecraft-hybrid.plain_explanation: Like a captain, field coordinator and players sharing work: Astra plans, Jev reacts to immediate events, and local policies turn decisions into movement and aiming. The footage reflects the entire system.
minecraft-hybrid.mechanism: The author explains that GPT-6 Astra handles longer-term goals, Jev reacts to events such as zombie attacks, and local policy models handle movement and aiming. Observation encoding, model frequencies and execution libraries are undisclosed.
minecraft-hybrid.advantage: Makes the planning, reactive-decision and low-level-control split explicit; useful to compare with the layered Pac-Man implementation.
minecraft-hybrid.limitation: Combat performance cannot be attributed to Jev alone. No Jev-only, Astra-only or combined-system comparison is available. The main video is approximately 2× speed; an original-speed version is supplied separately. No completion or speedrun result is established.
minecraft-hybrid.reported_result: The author demonstrates encounters with multiple zombies, explains the three layers in a reply and posts an original-speed version of the same footage.
minecraft-hybrid.media_note: The main video is about 192 seconds; the author-labeled original-speed version is about 384 seconds. Use the latter when judging responsiveness rather than inferring speed from the main clip.
minecraft-hybrid.review_summary: The author discloses planning, judgment and local movement policies plus an original-speed clip. The sped-up main clip cannot measure reaction time, and combined combat performance cannot be attributed to Jev alone.

emoji-suggestions.title: Live emoji suggestions
emoji-suggestions.summary: Suggest emoji that fit the meaning of text as it is entered.
emoji-suggestions.plain_explanation: The model selects from existing emoji rather than drawing new ones. The interface displays candidates and scores and asks again when the input changes. The exact question format is undisclosed.
emoji-suggestions.mechanism: The demo maps entered text to emoji candidates and scores. Its publisher compares response times with 3 and 200 candidates; API primitives, caching and request strategy are undisclosed.
emoji-suggestions.advantage: A bounded output space with immediately visible feedback; simpler than the repeated selection loop in character-by-character chat.
emoji-suggestions.limitation: The 100–200ms and candidate-count claims describe this demo, not arbitrary scales. No language, ambiguity or emoji-relevance evaluation is available.
emoji-suggestions.reported_result: The publisher reports roughly 100–200ms responses and similar speed with 3 or 200 candidates, in a roughly 13-second video.
emoji-suggestions.media_note: The main video shows text entry, emoji candidates and scores. No verified code entry point is recorded.
emoji-suggestions.review_summary: The demo reports 100–200 ms with similar timings for 3 and 200 candidates. Without repeated measurements or semantic accuracy, this does not imply constant latency at arbitrary scale.

voice-gesture-canvas.title: Voice-and-pointing canvas control
voice-gesture-canvas.summary: Use speech and pointing together to say “put that over there” on a canvas.
voice-gesture-canvas.plain_explanation: The app records where you point when saying words such as “that” and “there,” then asks Jev a few separate questions. It avoids enumerating every object, action and position combination as one huge choice list.
voice-gesture-canvas.mechanism: According to the author’s reply, the app captures pointing at key words and splits each sentence into a few small questions for Jev to confirm, then executes canvas actions. The video interface displays speech, finger and canvas state; perception libraries are undisclosed.
voice-gesture-canvas.advantage: Combines language and pointing to resolve references missing from text alone. Compared with TypeGPU’s semantic effects, this example focuses on manipulating canvas objects.
voice-gesture-canvas.limitation: The author explicitly describes an imperfect feasibility experiment. No pointing-error, speech-error or action-success evaluation is available, and separate decisions still require consistency checks.
voice-gesture-canvas.reported_result: The author shares a roughly 39-second canvas demo and explains pointing capture and question decomposition in a reply.
voice-gesture-canvas.media_note: The video interface shows a canvas, camera and separate input/decision panels. Implementation details come from the author’s reply; this is not evidence that Jev directly recognizes video.
voice-gesture-canvas.review_summary: The author explains keyword-timed pointing and several small judgments, explicitly admitting imperfect behavior. Perception libraries, success rates and recovery are unreported; the demo is a feasibility experiment.

youtube-sponsor-skip.title: YouTube sponsor-segment skipping
youtube-sponsor-skip.summary: Detect spoken sponsor segments while watching YouTube and jump past them.
youtube-sponsor-skip.plain_explanation: Like marking up captions: Jev identifies sponsor lines, code maps their IDs to playback times, then seeks the player. Listening modes first use a separate speech service to turn audio into text.
youtube-sponsor-skip.mechanism: The pinned source labels caption lines, scans windows for sponsor presence and boundaries with Jev, and maps selected lines to timestamps in code. Smart/Listen modes use Deepgram transcription and Jev judgments about the current segment. Code owns timestamp calculation and playback seeking.
youtube-sponsor-skip.advantage: Handles spoken sponsorship inside a video rather than hiding webpage ads. Transcript, hybrid and listening modes accommodate different caption availability.
youtube-sponsor-skip.limitation: Caption fetching can break; stepwise listening-mode seeks may overshoot into normal content. The author’s roughly $0.005/video claim is not universal across modes, and transcription adds cost. No accuracy or time-saving benchmark was run here.
youtube-sponsor-skip.reported_result: The author shares a roughly 21-second Chrome-extension demo, reports real-time detection at about $0.005/video, and calls it an open-source BYOK prototype.
youtube-sponsor-skip.media_note: The source video demonstrates the extension prototype. The repository’s web app and extension are one project, not two catalog entries.
youtube-sponsor-skip.source_notes: **Source review:** Read the pinned [README at de01f05](https://github.com/trungdq88/youtube-sponsor-detection/blob/de01f0568d043035889a296a61ce21e0accc8b16/README.md) and [src/jev.js](https://github.com/trungdq88/youtube-sponsor-detection/blob/de01f0568d043035889a296a61ce21e0accc8b16/src/jev.js). Documentation distinguishes hourly costs across modes and Deepgram’s per-minute charge. The post’s per-video estimate is not treated as a total-cost guarantee. No extension was installed or API called.
youtube-sponsor-skip.review_summary: Pinned code supports the transcript-line and audio-transcription implementation. This does not verify accuracy: audio modes incur extra costs and may overshoot, and the advertised per-video cost is not universal.

predictive-spreadsheet.title: Intent-driven spreadsheet ratings
predictive-spreadsheet.summary: Name a column “Urgency” and have the text in each row receive a corresponding rating.
predictive-spreadsheet.plain_explanation: Ordinary formulas calculate numbers; this demo uses a column name to express a question. Jev judges each row’s urgency, and the app writes the result into the table.
predictive-spreadsheet.mechanism: The author describes column intent and row content driving Jev ratings that update with typing. Question construction, score ranges, batching and caching are undisclosed.
predictive-spreadsheet.advantage: Brings semantic judgments into a familiar spreadsheet interface for experiments with ticket or text-record triage; emphasizes interaction beyond fixed-label batch classification.
predictive-spreadsheet.limitation: The roughly 100ms claim lacks row-count and timing-scope details. Ambiguous column names, rating consistency and large-table costs are unevaluated. Arbitrary headings are not proven to become reliable formulas.
predictive-spreadsheet.reported_result: The author shares a roughly 18-second video, reporting ratings from no follow-up needed to urgent after entering Urgency, in roughly 100ms.
predictive-spreadsheet.media_note: Uses this spreadsheet post’s own video, not the launcher video it quotes.
predictive-spreadsheet.source_notes: **Deduplication:** This post quotes the same author’s launcher, but has its own video and a different task: rating spreadsheet rows rather than ranking files. It is a separate data-classification case; common authorship or a quote alone does not establish duplicate identity.
predictive-spreadsheet.review_summary: A concrete intent-labelled spreadsheet demo; question construction, consistency and timing scope are unknown, so arbitrary-column reliability is not established.

probably-language.title: Probably: semantic judgments as program control
probably-language.summary: Write judgments such as “is this email urgent?” into branches, then ask a text model to draft a reply.
probably-language.plain_explanation: Put a judgment inside a program: Jev decides whether a condition holds or which branch fits, an interpreter coordinates the steps, and a separate model writes text.
probably-language.mechanism: The Probably 0.1 website describes a TypeScript interpreter: feels asks Jev about conditions, match selects a descriptive branch, while repeats judgments, and llm calls a separate text model. Conditions support confidence gates; match has no confidence gate in this version.
probably-language.advantage: Combines classification, branching and revision loops in a readable small language. Useful alongside vocabulary-chat and RISC-jeV experiments for understanding composition.
probably-language.limitation: Explicitly a toy language without general-purpose features such as arrays or functions. The hosted playground replays recorded results; custom programs require local execution with live model providers. Playback speed is not an inference benchmark.
probably-language.reported_result: The author posts a language-example image and playground URL, describing feels, match and while, with Jev making judgments and an LLM writing.
probably-language.media_note: The main post includes a language-example image. The website was read; programs were not executed and cached demonstrations were not treated as live API tests.
probably-language.source_notes: **Website review:** [Probably 0.1](https://probably-lang.southpolesteve.workers.dev) states that its hosted Worker replays bundled recordings and rejects uncached custom code or inputs without model calls. The interpreter also limits model calls and loop iterations per run. These are documented behaviors, not results from running the local interpreter.
probably-language.review_summary: The site documents interpreter, Jev and text-model responsibilities and toy-language limits. Hosted examples replay cached results; custom inputs require local live calls. This disclosed replay is not a live speed benchmark.

eslint-rule-judgments.title: Code judgments from ESLint rule descriptions
eslint-rule-judgments.summary: Give Jev a rule’s text description and ask whether a small code snippet complies.
eslint-rule-judgments.plain_explanation: Like handing a reviewer a marking guide and a snippet: Jev judges whether the rule is violated. The experiment interprets the rule’s meaning rather than executing its ESLint implementation.
eslint-rule-judgments.mechanism: The author says Jev receives ESLint descriptions without their implementations. A later reply clarifies that the experiment uses generated small snippets and the code is being organized. Complete inputs, sample construction and evaluation protocol remain unverified.
eslint-rule-judgments.advantage: Explores turning written rules into quick code judgments. More focused than general PR scoring and suitable for comparison with deterministic lint results.
eslint-rule-judgments.limitation: The roughly 90% correctness claim concerns the author’s snippet experiment, not whole repositories or real PRs. Public samples, independent evaluation and per-rule false positives/negatives are still needed. It provides no deterministic-linter guarantee.
eslint-rule-judgments.reported_result: The author posts a results screenshot claiming roughly 90% correct judgments, then clarifies that the inputs are generated small snippets rather than whole repositories.
eslint-rule-judgments.media_note: The source image is the author’s experimental report, not output generated by this repository.
eslint-rule-judgments.review_summary: The author scopes the result to generated snippets. The roughly 90% figure is self-reported and cannot be extrapolated to repository-wide linting reliability.

opencode-intent-permissions.title: OpenCode intent-aware permissions
opencode-intent-permissions.summary: Check an agent’s actions across tools using policies such as “only access Google.”
opencode-intent-permissions.plain_explanation: Like a gatekeeper considering both access rules and the purpose of a request: Jev judges tool-input intent, and the plugin allows, asks or denies. Native OpenCode permissions remain the outer layer.
opencode-intent-permissions.mechanism: The oc-auto-perms 0.1.0 documentation sends selected tool inputs, policies and recent requests to Jev, using ordered rules for allow/ask/deny. Low confidence or API failure becomes ask. Native deny stays denied and native ask still prompts; Jev further restricts native allow.
opencode-intent-permissions.advantage: Expresses a shared semantic restriction across shell, webfetch and other tools without enumerating every command. Goes beyond risk scoring by participating in permission decisions.
opencode-intent-permissions.limitation: The video does not establish bypass resistance; deterministic hard boundaries remain necessary. Version 0.1.0 explicitly excludes Code Mode execute and sends policies, recent user messages and tool inputs to TypeSafe. No adversarial or permission tests were run here.
opencode-intent-permissions.reported_result: The author demonstrates a Google-only policy and reports blocking the shown attempts; the main post now has 235 likes at retrieval.
opencode-intent-permissions.media_note: The main post includes a roughly 91-second video and configuration image. Eligibility uses the author’s post, without adding repost likes.
opencode-intent-permissions.source_notes: **Promoted from the inbox:** The 2026-09-18 02:38:04 UTC snapshot had 160 likes; the 06:07:34 UTC snapshot has 235 and now qualifies. The [author’s reply](https://x.com/OpeOginni/status/2100705405013754312) links the package. Read [npm metadata and README](https://registry.npmjs.org/oc-auto-perms), whose latest version was 0.1.0. The plugin was not installed.
opencode-intent-permissions.review_summary: The every-route wording refers to the demonstrated attempts, so B rather than C. Published docs explicitly expose a Code Mode bypass and preserve native permission controls; the demo is not a universal network boundary.

email-speed-race.title: Email classification: four-model speed comparison
email-speed-race.summary: Classify a set of emails with four models and compare progress and elapsed time on one screen.
email-speed-race.plain_explanation: Like four sorting clerks handling the same stack of letters: each model assigns categories while the page tracks results and time. This demonstration focuses on speed; finishing first does not mean every label is correct.
email-speed-race.mechanism: The source video’s JEV Speed Race interface places Jev, GPT Luna, Claude Sonnet and Gemini 3.5 Flash side by side, with matching email rows, progress counters and timers. This establishes a task-level speed comparison; request settings, full model versions and classification rules remain unverified.
email-speed-race.advantage: Makes differences in waiting time across models more visible than a single-model batch demo. Compare it with the 500-email case to distinguish cross-model responsiveness from batch throughput.
email-speed-race.limitation: No independent accuracy, confusion-matrix or full-cost evaluation is available. Concurrency, batching and timing conditions remain unverified, and interface labels do not establish exact API versions. This is insufficient for a universal speed ranking or multiplier.
email-speed-race.reported_result: The author shares a roughly 30-second comparison video and reports Jev as substantially faster. This repository has not reproduced that claim or treated video length as classification latency.
email-speed-race.media_note: Uses this post’s own video and thumbnail. The source interface and discussion were inspected; this is not a repost of the existing 500-email video.
email-speed-race.source_notes: **Deduplication and comparison:** The author, interface and source video differ from Riley Brown’s batch-email case, so this is a separate experiment in the same category. Without a shared complete test protocol, advertised times and costs should not be compared directly.
email-speed-race.review_summary: A task-level speed demo is visible, but unspecified model versions, concurrency and accuracy prevent a general performance ranking.

code-comment-scoring.title: Code comments: accuracy and usefulness scores
code-comment-scoring.summary: Check whether a comment is correct and whether it adds useful information beyond the code.
code-comment-scoring.plain_explanation: Give each comment two report cards: it may correctly restate the code without explaining why it exists, or even misdescribe what the code does. Jev scores the dimensions separately to highlight comments worth reviewing.
code-comment-scoring.mechanism: The source terminal screenshot shows two small code/comment examples with 0–100 Accuracy and Usefulness scores and descriptions. The observable flow takes code plus comments into judgments and displays scores; prompts, parsing and score mapping are not established by the available evidence.
code-comment-scoring.advantage: Separating factual correctness from informational value makes issues easier to interpret than a single overall code score. Like the ESLint experiment, it examines local code, but evaluates comment quality rather than rule compliance.
code-comment-scoring.limitation: Two trivial examples do not establish performance on complex code. Scores are not independently measured test accuracy, and automatic comment deletion or rewriting is not demonstrated. The author describes a possible gate for reducing larger-model review, not a complete reviewer.
code-comment-scoring.reported_result: The screenshot gives a correct but redundant multiplication comment 99/100 for accuracy and 2/100 for usefulness. A comment describing division as multiplication receives 1/100 and 11/100. The author confirms both lack informational value and the second is also wrong.
code-comment-scoring.media_note: The source image is the author’s terminal experiment output. Two author replies clarify the scores and proposed screening role.
code-comment-scoring.source_notes: **Promoted after fourth-pass evidence review:** Previously pending because the label meanings were unclear. Image inspection and author replies establish two scoring dimensions and just two examples. Included as a concrete task experiment, not described as a shipped linter or mature product; no verifiable source-code entry point was obtained in this review.
code-comment-scoring.review_summary: Two simple examples illustrate separate accuracy and usefulness scores, and the author positions it as a gate. These scores are not evaluation accuracy or validation on complex code.

runlayer-adversarial-testing.title: Runlayer: parallel adversarial browser testing
runlayer-adversarial-testing.summary: Run multiple browser sessions to explore how a new release might fail during use.
runlayer-adversarial-testing.plain_explanation: Like a team of testers trying software at once: Jev contributes quick decisions while agents and browsers perform actions. Proving a defect still requires a clear failure criterion and reproducible steps.
runlayer-adversarial-testing.mechanism: The author identifies Runlayer agents, agent-browser and Chromium; the source video shows a matrix of browser windows. Jev is used in adversarial release testing, but observation formats, task distribution, path deduplication, assertions and defect-report structures are undisclosed.
runlayer-adversarial-testing.advantage: Emphasizes concurrent exploration of interaction paths. Compare it with the existing OpenCode testing demo for parallel exploration versus post-development acceptance checks. Author replies identify the tooling for further investigation.
runlayer-adversarial-testing.limitation: Many windows do not establish broad path coverage. Concurrency, real defect detection, retries and full-run costs are unspecified. The author’s “pennies” description is not a per-test cost guarantee.
runlayer-adversarial-testing.reported_result: The author shares a roughly 14-second multi-browser video, describes attempts to break each release and reports low cost, without an independent defect-detection evaluation.
runlayer-adversarial-testing.media_note: Uses the main post’s multi-window video and two author replies about the stack. Windows and tool components are not counted as separate applications.
runlayer-adversarial-testing.review_summary: The parallel browser setup is plausible, but window count and low-cost wording do not establish meaningful coverage or defect-detection effectiveness.

hono-semantic-router.title: Hono JevRouter: route requests by meaning
hono-semantic-router.summary: Choose responses such as HTML or Markdown based on whether a request appears to come from a person or an AI.
hono-semantic-router.plain_explanation: Ordinary routing sorts letters by address; this experiment also considers their meaning. Developers describe handlers in words, Jev judges each description, and code selects the first qualifying handler in registration order.
hono-semantic-router.mechanism: Pinned code builds state from the method, URL, headers and a truncated textual body, then asks one Noul question per route in a single call. The first registered route reaching the threshold wins (default 0.5), not the highest-scoring route. Ordinary path handlers can respond first; no semantic match falls through to not-found handling.
hono-semantic-router.advantage: Explores intent-sensitive responses alongside ordinary Hono routing. Unlike model routing, it chooses HTTP handlers, making the resulting behavior easier to inspect.
hono-semantic-router.limitation: Explicitly experimental and unsuitable as an authentication or authorization boundary. Semantic routing adds model latency and cost. Request content is sent to Jev; only specified sensitive headers are redacted by default. Route order and adversarial input can affect outcomes.
hono-semantic-router.reported_result: The author shares a usage-code image, playground and open-source package. The example serves Markdown to AI requests and HTML to human browsers. The latest npm version during this review was 0.2.0; it was not installed or tested.
hono-semantic-router.media_note: The source image shows usage code, not a performance benchmark. An author reply directly links the repository.
hono-semantic-router.source_notes: **Source review:** Read the [README at 04f6e10](https://github.com/yusukebe/hono-jev-router/blob/04f6e103e1397bca659ab85c042011a1f14b679d/README.md) and [src/index.ts](https://github.com/yusukebe/hono-jev-router/blob/04f6e103e1397bca659ab85c042011a1f14b679d/src/index.ts). Route probabilities are independent and need not sum to one; these are multiple yes/no judgments, not mutually exclusive classification. No playground request was submitted.
hono-semantic-router.review_summary: The source directly supports first-matching semantic routing and explicitly states its limits. It is an inspectable routing experiment, not an authentication guarantee.

sac-calendar-computer-use.title: Sac: Codex + Jev for Mac Calendar
sac-calendar-computer-use.summary: Add a Jev decision layer to Codex computer use and compare creating a calendar event side by side.

sac-calendar-computer-use.mechanism: The newly published version extracts text candidates from the accessibility tree. Jev judges targets, actions, completion and risk; Codex Computer Use observes and executes. Code checks candidate validity, confidence and policy gates. Sending text instead of screenshots does not mean offline processing.
sac-calendar-computer-use.advantage: A concrete shared task makes pauses easy to observe and adds a desktop-workflow experiment alongside existing browser and OCR examples.
sac-calendar-computer-use.limitation: One calendar demo does not establish average speedup, success rate or total cost. Source improves inspectability, but the new fastest-in-Codex claim lacks a matched task benchmark. This catalog has not run the tool.
sac-calendar-computer-use.reported_result: The author shares a roughly 51-second video labeled 1× playback, reports smoother operation with similar token usage, and clarifies in a reply that Jev makes judgments within existing computer use. The update publishes Jev-cu and claims larger gains for tasks with frequent decisions and tool calls, without a new reproducible timing comparison.
sac-calendar-computer-use.media_note: Uses this post’s own Calendar comparison video, not the quoted post’s generic product image. The 1× label is shown on screen; timing was not independently verified.

Cataloged as this author’s experiment; a similar name does not establish Cua usage. The quoted introductory roundup is not a separate case.
sac-calendar-computer-use.review_summary: Text candidates and execution roles are inspectable, but the new fastest-in-Codex comparison lacks a matched benchmark. C addresses that superlative, not prototype existence.

shell-history-suggestions.title: Shell history: semantic command suggestions
shell-history-suggestions.summary: Type part of a command or describe an intent to select a suggestion from past commands.
shell-history-suggestions.plain_explanation: Like a history menu that understands meaning: code lists previous commands and Jev picks the closest to your intent. Code controls candidates, matching and display; the user accepts a suggestion into the command line.
shell-history-suggestions.mechanism: The pinned README describes a zsh plugin using the latest 100 distinct history entries, narrowing to prefix matches when available. A single prefix candidate skips the model. Otherwise Choice selects a command ID and Noul judges whether any candidate fits; thresholds gate suggestions and stale responses are discarded after input changes.
shell-history-suggestions.advantage: Supports intent descriptions beyond literal prefixes while restricting outputs to historical candidates. Like the predictive launcher it selects candidates, but operates on commands rather than files.
shell-history-suggestions.limitation: History can be stale or sensitive and is sent to the service as candidate data. A suitable suggestion does not establish safe execution; user review remains necessary. The README reports roughly 0.7–0.9 seconds per request, not the millisecond claims from other demos. The author presents an experiment, not evidence of daily use.
shell-history-suggestions.reported_result: The author shares a roughly 22-second demo and repository, then states that Amp produced the demo. The repository README explicitly says it uses fabricated command history.
shell-history-suggestions.media_note: The main video and the author’s Amp production video are one project. A demonstration with fabricated history is not a real-user-log evaluation.
shell-history-suggestions.source_notes: **Documentation review:** Read the [README at 4b2b75d](https://github.com/mrnugget/jev-shell-history/blob/4b2b75d26c0ccf5726263904514a22a8e11659ea/README.md), distinguishing prefix filtering, Jev candidate judgments and zsh acceptance. The plugin was not installed and local shell history was not transmitted.
shell-history-suggestions.review_summary: Pinned docs specify history candidates, prefix filtering, Choice/Noul gates and stale-result rejection. The demo uses fabricated history and reports 0.7–0.9 s latency; everyday adoption and long-term acceptance are not established.

calorie-notebook.title: Calorie Notebook: text-based food logging
calorie-notebook.summary: Write down what you ate and receive quick calorie, nutrient and total values in the interface.
calorie-notebook.plain_explanation: Like putting an estimator beside a notebook: food and portion descriptions become numerical feedback. The author says Jev is used, but the food-data source and calculation method are not disclosed here.
calorie-notebook.mechanism: The video shows Calorie Notebook with food-text rows, calorie and nutrient values, and totals. The observable interaction maps text to structured numbers; Jev question types, food-database lookup, portion handling and aggregation remain unverified.
calorie-notebook.advantage: Emphasizes feedback while entering food, potentially reducing item-by-item logging effort. Compare responsiveness with the predictive spreadsheet, while separately checking portion interpretation and numerical evidence.
calorie-notebook.limitation: No database, recipe handling or error evaluation against actual labels is disclosed; an author reply also notes limitations of model calorie estimation. Fast responses do not establish accurate calories or a reliable nutrition-measurement tool.
calorie-notebook.reported_result: The author shares a roughly 41-second food-logging video and reports instant feedback. The interface shows food text, calorie and nutrient totals without a complete latency or estimation-accuracy benchmark.
calorie-notebook.media_note: The source video shows a distinct food-logging interface. The same author’s included Skillbox, filter and PR tools serve different tasks and are not merged or counted again.
calorie-notebook.review_summary: The interface is demonstrated, and the author expressly concedes estimation limitations. Instant numerical output does not establish nutritional accuracy.

compact-adviser.title: Compact Adviser: choose when to compact
compact-adviser.summary: Suggest when a coding conversation has reached a suitable point for context compaction.
compact-adviser.plain_explanation: Like a secretary choosing a pause between topics for meeting notes: Jev judges timing and the host performs compaction. It does not select passages for deletion.
compact-adviser.mechanism: Pinned documentation uses two yes/no judgments about work-unit completion and hands-on versus coordination work. Code combines them with context usage, token floors and cooldowns. Pi and Claude support optional automatic mode; Codex CLI is advisory only.
compact-adviser.advantage: Complements tool-output compaction by deciding when it should happen. Documented gates and fallbacks make the policy inspectable.

Implementation descriptions above come from documentation, not installation, execution or independent reproduction.

json-render-ui.title: json-render: assemble interfaces from component choices
json-render-ui.summary: Turn interface requests into constrained component layouts, including additions, removals and moves.

json-render-ui.reported_result: The author shares an editable UI video and source links. Documentation rules out freeform generation calls; independent quality comparisons are absent.
json-render-ui.media_note: The main video and author’s source-code reply form one case; quote-posts are not additional applications.
json-render-ui.source_notes: **Documentation review:** Read the [pinned documentation](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/3ad381881194e7011ad3ccd6d668033495a06c29/apps/web/lib/jev/README.md). Implementation descriptions above come from documentation, not installation, execution or independent reproduction.
json-render-ui.review_summary: Pinned docs substantiate component selection, staged layout and JSON assembly in code, without full-page templates or freeform generation. “Instant” is not established for arbitrary UIs: candidates, text, batch size and depth are bounded, with no matched-quality end-to-end benchmark.

seo-internal-links.title: SEO internal links: match existing text to relevant pages
seo-internal-links.summary: Scan site articles and suggest relevant internal links using text already present.
seo-internal-links.plain_explanation: Like an editor marking where an article could link to another: Jev judges relevance and code pairs existing text with destination pages.
seo-internal-links.mechanism: The author describes yes/no judgments for page relevance and existing anchor text: 586 pages and 8,790 judgments. Full candidate retrieval and write-back details are undisclosed.
seo-internal-links.advantage: Unlike content-popularity scores, it produces concrete suggestions editors can inspect, including decisions to add no link.

box-incident-triage.title: Box: triage and file incident reports
box-incident-triage.summary: Read incident reports, judge impact and severity, and route them to handling folders.

snack-scoring.title: NoSugarForKids: multi-criterion snack scoring
snack-scoring.summary: Score children’s snacks in batches to organize a product catalog.

tax-doc-classifier.title: Tax Doc Classifier: label tax PDF pages

Implementation descriptions above come from documentation, not installation, execution or independent reproduction.

ego-product-decisions.title: ego lite: filter Amazon products
ego-product-decisions.summary: Combine browser tooling and models to filter products on a webpage.

cnvs-voice-gate.title: CNVS: gate voice commands without a wake word

tester-army-e2e.title: Tester Army: web and mobile end-to-end testing
tester-army-e2e.summary: Explore agent-driven interface tests in a framework targeting web and mobile.

ai-hedge-fund-backtest.title: AI Hedge Fund: strategy backtesting
ai-hedge-fund-backtest.summary: Choose a strategy and stock tickers to run an experiment on historical data.

ocr-image-organizer.title: OCR + Jev: organize images
ocr-image-organizer.summary: Read text from images, then categorize them by content.
ocr-image-organizer.plain_explanation: Like copying words from a photo onto a card before sorting cards: OCR reads the words and Jev judges categories.
ocr-image-organizer.mechanism: The author explicitly combines OCR and Jev for 900 images. The OCR engine, taxonomy, confidence policy and file-operation rules are undisclosed.
ocr-image-organizer.advantage: Shares text extraction with CoreML/OCR desktop clicking, but produces image categories rather than action coordinates.
ocr-image-organizer.limitation: Text-free images and OCR errors limit classification. This is not direct image understanding by Jev, and accuracy across image types is unmeasured.
ocr-image-organizer.reported_result: The author reports roughly 40 seconds for 900 images; cost and end-to-end timing boundaries are unclear.
ocr-image-organizer.media_note: The source includes about 62 seconds of demonstration; video duration differs from reported processing time.
ocr-image-organizer.review_summary: The stated OCR-plus-classifier design is plausible; category accuracy and timing boundaries are unspecified, and the demo does not establish native image understanding by Jev.

game-level-generation.title: Sprite Fusion: generate runner terrain in real time
game-level-generation.summary: Select new platforms and gaps ahead of a moving player.
game-level-generation.plain_explanation: Like giving a level designer a box of fixed-size tiles: Jev chooses width, gap, height and surface type, and game code places them.
game-level-generation.mechanism: The author’s article supplies player position, velocity, dash state and terrain, then asks parallel choice questions for the next four surfaces. PhaserJS builds terrain; Sprite Fusion separately provides graphical assets.
game-level-generation.advantage: Unlike Mario or Flappy Bird action selection, this creates the environment. Bounded tile choices support collision and reachability checks.
game-level-generation.limitation: A simple runner prototype without long-horizon playability or adaptive-difficulty evaluation. Asset generation and terrain decisions are separate stages.
game-level-generation.reported_result: The author records five requests at 319–375 ms Jev latency and an estimated $0.00057 each, not a measured sub-100 ms system.
game-level-generation.media_note: The main video, implementation article and author’s state clarification form one case.
game-level-generation.source_notes: **Author article:** The [implementation write-up](https://www.spritefusion.com/blog/generating-game-level-in-real-time-with-jev) documents allowed surface types, widths, gaps, heights and a recorded response. This is public-design analysis; the game was not run.
game-level-generation.review_summary: The implementation article specifies state, finite terrain choices and code placement, with five measured requests at 319–375ms. This supports bounded terrain assembly, not asset generation, unrestricted game creation or long-term playability.

maxfusion-ad-classifier.title: MaxFusion: classify advertising creatives
maxfusion-ad-classifier.summary: Label ads by style and customer-journey stage for account-level analysis.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.plain_explanation: Like arranging ads in a labeled cabinet: Jev judges dimensions and code aggregates results. Labels do not establish campaign effectiveness.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.mechanism: The author reports classifying 1,891 Resilia ads by journey stage, style and other dimensions. Text extraction, visual preprocessing and label definitions are not fully disclosed.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.advantage: Compare with StealAds for ad organization. This reports a larger batch, but different data, labels and preprocessing prevent direct timing comparisons.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.limitation: Human-label agreement, campaign impact and full collection costs are absent. Announced MCP support is not confirmed as released.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.reported_result: The author reports 1,891 ads in 19 seconds for $0.12; not independently reproduced.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.media_note: A distinct author, product and video differentiate it from StealAds despite their shared purpose.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.review_summary: A specific ad-classification demo, with no validated label accuracy or complete preprocessing costs; batch size does not prove superiority over another tool.

danish-stock-backtest.title: Danish equities: a full-year historical strategy experiment
danish-stock-backtest.summary: Experiment with trading decisions on 2025 market data using news and other signals.
danish-stock-backtest.plain_explanation: Like working through an old market diary one day at a time. A valid backtest must restrict inputs to information available at each historical moment.
danish-stock-backtest.mechanism: The author cites market data, news, Wikipedia and Google Trends sentiment. Published in 2026 about 2025, it is cataloged as historical experimentation; time cutoffs and execution details are unknown.
danish-stock-backtest.advantage: Identifies multiple input sources and a year-long span, complementing the configuration-focused backtest interface.
danish-stock-backtest.limitation: Look-ahead controls, fees, slippage and reliable return statistics are missing. Token charges are not full strategy costs.
danish-stock-backtest.reported_result: The author reports 239 trading days, 8.1 million tokens and $0.32; not independently reproduced.
danish-stock-backtest.media_note: The roughly 22-second video is not evidence of current live-account trading.
danish-stock-backtest.review_summary: The dated 2025 run is a historical experiment with self-reported token cost. Point-in-time inputs, leakage controls, trading costs and validated returns are unspecified; it is not evidence of profitable live trading.

flappy-bird.title: Flappy Bird: navigate obstacles
flappy-bird.summary: Use Jev in controlling a bird through obstacles.
flappy-bird.plain_explanation: Think of repeatedly asking whether to flap now. This is an explanatory analogy; how this demo supplies state and schedules decisions is undisclosed.
flappy-bird.mechanism: The author posts Jev playing Flappy Bird without specifying observations, action frequency or whether the environment pauses for inference.
flappy-bird.advantage: A simpler action space than many character games helps study timing, but does not itself establish reliability.
flappy-bird.limitation: No multi-run scores, failure clips, costs or reproducible source. A successful clip does not establish completion rate.
flappy-bird.reported_result: The author supplies roughly 49 seconds of gameplay without a verifiable quantitative success rate.
flappy-bird.media_note: Cataloged as a distinct game task alongside other game-decision experiments.
flappy-bird.review_summary: A plausible short game-control demo. The effortless framing is impressionistic; observation format, timing, failures and repeated scores are not available.

script-code-review.title: Script.it: flag issues before writing review comments
script-code-review.summary: Score a git diff first, then ask a language model for explanations only when issues are flagged.
script-code-review.plain_explanation: Like marking suspicious changes with a checklist before asking a reviewer to explain them. This can avoid lengthy exploration but may miss deeper issues.
script-code-review.mechanism: The author replaces a multi-turn GLM/Grok/Gemini ensemble with direct Jev scoring of raw diffs, invoking an LLM for explanations after a flag.
script-code-review.advantage: Explicitly separates detection from explanation compared with agent-led review, and discloses the recall tradeoff.
script-code-review.limitation: The private set’s size and labels are unavailable. Zero false positives refers to tested developer-disputed findings, not a guarantee of no production errors.
script-code-review.reported_result: The author reports roughly 50× speed, 100× cost improvement and 75% confirmed-bug recall; the previous ensemble detected more bugs.
script-code-review.media_note: The source includes an image and workflow description. Results remain an internal author evaluation, not independent certification.
script-code-review.review_summary: The author discloses the workflow change and 75% recall trade-off. Private-data zero false positives and speed/cost ratios remain unverified, but are not presented as an equal-recall universal guarantee.

nifty-trading.title: Nifty intraday trading: an account demo with a stop-loss report
nifty-trading.summary: Demonstrate Jev-connected Nifty trading and report a triggered stop loss.
nifty-trading.plain_explanation: Like connecting decisions to orders with a stopping rule. Model judgments, broker execution and risk controls have separate roles; a video does not prove profitability.
nifty-trading.mechanism: The author claims a real Kotak account with ₹100,000 and 5× leverage. Strategy inputs, Jev candidates and order code are undisclosed; live-account status was not independently verified.
nifty-trading.advantage: Unlike speed-only trading posts, this discloses a stopped-out day and an author-reported adverse outcome.
nifty-trading.limitation: Accounts, fills and net returns are unverified. Leverage magnifies losses; one stop-loss report does not establish durable risk control.
nifty-trading.reported_result: The author says an initially profitable morning ended at the ₹1,000 hard stop, not an overall profitable day.
nifty-trading.media_note: The roughly 38-second video has a different author, market and execution venue from the Monad/Kuru bot.
nifty-trading.review_summary: The source reports a stop-loss after an initially green morning, not a profitable day. Account authenticity, executions and long-term risk controls remain unverified; the disclosure is more balanced than profit marketing.

downloads-organizer.title: macOS Downloads: organize files by rules
downloads-organizer.summary: Watch Downloads and move matching files to destinations defined by custom rules.
downloads-organizer.plain_explanation: Like a clerk recognizing an invoice and filing it: Jev judges rules, while the application moves and names files.
downloads-organizer.mechanism: The author demonstrates macOS folder monitoring and customizable rules, including invoice recognition and filing. They report no other LLM calls; extraction and filename construction are undisclosed.
downloads-organizer.advantage: Fits an ongoing local-file workflow rather than only batch classification. Box triage instead handles business reports in cloud folders.
downloads-organizer.limitation: Wrong moves or names can impair retrieval. Undo, conflicts, permissions and classification accuracy are undocumented.
downloads-organizer.reported_result: The author supplies a roughly nine-second demo without long-term or quantitative classification results.
downloads-organizer.media_note: Distinct from the same author’s X filter because both task and video differ.
downloads-organizer.review_summary: A plausible file-rule automation; extraction and filename construction are undisclosed, and no-other-LLM does not imply free-form generation by Jev.

color-judgments.title: Words and colors: visualize 16-color judgments
color-judgments.summary: Enter words and visualize the model’s judgments about colors.
color-judgments.plain_explanation: Like putting “tomato” into a box of 16 crayons: Jev weights color candidates and code visualizes the weights. It is not recognizing colors from photographs.
color-judgments.mechanism: Author replies specify 16 predefined static colors and link the palette. The complete display mapping is undocumented; separate RGB-mixing trials belong to the same experiment.
color-judgments.advantage: A smaller candidate set than pixel drawing offers direct semantic feedback for exploring word-to-visual interaction.
color-judgments.limitation: Constrained by palette and prompts, subjective associations have no single correct answer. This is not an image-recognition or color-science evaluation.
color-judgments.reported_result: The author shares roughly 65 seconds of interaction and palette details, without quantitative evaluation.
color-judgments.media_note: The 16-color explanation and later mixing discussion are merged rather than counted as multiple apps.
color-judgments.review_summary: The author discloses a fixed 16-color palette and rendering weighted probabilities. This supports word-to-palette associations, not visual color recognition or color-science accuracy.

x-reply-cleanup.title: X reply cleanup: flag low-value comments
x-reply-cleanup.summary: Identify suspected low-value replies to help clean up a post’s discussion.
x-reply-cleanup.plain_explanation: Like marking likely spam while letting the user correct mistakes. The author says corrections inform later decisions; storage details are unknown.
x-reply-cleanup.mechanism: The video shows checked/flagged reply counts, and the author describes Jev-based cleanup with false-positive correction. Local hiding, account blocking or other action semantics were not established; deleting others’ comments is not claimed.
x-reply-cleanup.advantage: More focused on replies than general feed filtering, with a correction mechanism; distinct from this author’s historical-post analysis.
x-reply-cleanup.limitation: Low-value judgments are subjective and error rates are unavailable. Correction feedback does not establish model training or cross-user learning.
x-reply-cleanup.reported_result: The author supplies roughly 15 seconds of video and a quick-build claim, without formal filtering evaluation.
x-reply-cleanup.media_note: The main video and correction follow-up form one application.
x-reply-cleanup.review_summary: The demo supports reply flagging and correction, but the precise action is unclear; using feedback on a later call is not evidence of model training or measured accuracy.

claude-code-jev-router.title: Claude Code Mod: model and effort routing
claude-code-jev-router.summary: Choose subagent models and adjust reasoning effort in the main conversation.
claude-code-jev-router.plain_explanation: Like ticket triage: Jev judges task difficulty and the plugin assigns an assistant; the selected model still writes the code.
claude-code-jev-router.mechanism: Pinned code classifies at prompt submission and applies decisions at model requests and subagent creation. Subagent-model and main-effort routing default on; main-model switching defaults off. This differs from the post’s session-start-only description; the pinned implementation takes precedence.
claude-code-jev-router.advantage: Unlike the Codex router, this uses Claude Code hooks and separates main-session and subagent decisions, making cache and fallback policies inspectable.
claude-code-jev-router.limitation: No complete quality, cache-cost or savings comparison. Without a Jev key, the host classifier is used, so that path is not evidence of Jev performance.
claude-code-jev-router.reported_result: The post includes a roughly 25-second video; source supports TypeSafe or Vercel Gateway. It establishes a routing mechanism, not cheaper equivalent-quality completion.
claude-code-jev-router.media_note: Same purpose as the Codex router but a distinct repository, host, author and video; grouped as an independent implementation.
claude-code-jev-router.review_summary: Pinned source exposes hooks, defaults and fallback. Main-model behavior differs from the post’s description; savings remain unverified.

synthetic-interview-classifier.title: Synthetic interview notes: batch classification and scoring
synthetic-interview-classifier.summary: Sort 100 fictional interview records into advance, hold or decline and assign component scores.
synthetic-interview-classifier.plain_explanation: Like applying a checklist to fictional interview notes: judge skills, communication and interest, then organize the results. Scores do not establish real job performance.
synthetic-interview-classifier.mechanism: The author describes three outcomes, three scoring dimensions and serious-concern flags. Full prompts, rubrics and reference labels were not established.
synthetic-interview-classifier.advantage: Extends ordinary single-label text classification to several dimensions; synthetic records make the workflow easier to explore first.
synthetic-interview-classifier.limitation: No evidence of real hiring validity, fairness or label agreement; the demo does not justify automated personnel selection.
synthetic-interview-classifier.reported_result: The author reports 12.8 seconds and $0.005 for 100 fictional records: one batch test, not an accuracy evaluation.
synthetic-interview-classifier.media_note: The main post includes roughly 24 seconds of video. Department matching is a suggested future use, not an established feature.
synthetic-interview-classifier.review_summary: Explicitly fictional data supports a batch-classification demo; independent labels and error statistics are missing.

traffic-light-city.title: Jev City: nine-intersection traffic simulation
traffic-light-city.summary: Choose signal directions in a virtual road network and observe queues and waiting time.
traffic-light-city.plain_explanation: Like a dispatcher in a model city: code supplies junction state, Jev chooses a direction, and the simulator moves vehicles.
traffic-light-city.mechanism: The display shows nine junctions, north/south versus east/west decisions and confidence, an on/off control and wait curves. Full state encoding and the off-mode baseline were not established.
traffic-light-city.advantage: Unlike controlling one simulated car, this coordinates junctions to explore network-level congestion effects.
traffic-light-city.limitation: Matched traffic demand, seeds, repeated trials and fixed/adaptive rule baselines are missing. A virtual network does not establish real-city outcomes.
traffic-light-city.reported_result: The author claims average waiting rises by over 600% when Jev is switched off; a 73-second clip and public entry point do not verify that ratio.
traffic-light-city.media_note: The original simulation video and author’s entry-point reply form one case, distinct from this author’s X algorithm simulation.
traffic-light-city.review_summary: The over-600% claim lacks matched controller baselines and repeated statistics. The simulation interface does not establish real-world traffic gains.

vital-signs-simulator.title: Vital-sign simulation: judging state changes
vital-signs-simulator.summary: Compare rule alarms with Jev judgments in normal-state and slow-heart-rate simulations.
vital-signs-simulator.plain_explanation: Like a practice drill for a monitor: compare judgments on simulated measurements. Model confidence is not a clinically validated event probability.
vital-signs-simulator.mechanism: Two clips include movement artifacts and a slow-heart-rate scenario. Complete inputs, prediction horizon, reference labels and thresholds are undisclosed.
vital-signs-simulator.advantage: Unlike traffic or robotics control, this explores state assessment and false alarms; scenarios can inform later evaluation questions.
vital-signs-simulator.limitation: No clinical dataset, independent validation or missed-event statistics was provided. The author’s repeatability-based explanation of calibration does not establish risk-probability validity.
vital-signs-simulator.reported_result: The author reports better simulated behavior and says in a reply that it could be used in practice. Evidence is limited to two roughly 44/46-second simulation clips.
vital-signs-simulator.media_note: Both videos belong to one simulator. Replies about practical use and calibration support the assessment, not separate cases.
vital-signs-simulator.review_summary: Two simulations do not support readiness for practical use. Repeatability, confidence and clinical event probability are different validation targets.

dual-arm-robot-sim.title: Dual-arm robot simulation: layered action decisions
dual-arm-robot-sim.summary: Manipulate blocks in simulation, with Jev handling the middle decision layer.
dual-arm-robot-sim.plain_explanation: Like a supervisor choosing which block to move while an engineer calculates arm motion: decisions, joint solving and physics have separate roles.
dual-arm-robot-sim.mechanism: The author assigns layer two of three to Jev, with inverse kinematics and physics in code. Media shows simulated arms, blocks and an instruction panel.
dual-arm-robot-sim.advantage: Like drone simulation, this separates decisions from motion computation, but explores object selection and dual-arm manipulation.
dual-arm-robot-sim.limitation: No physical-robot deployment or complete success-rate evaluation. A roughly 500ms response is not a joint-control period or full task duration.
dual-arm-robot-sim.reported_result: The author reports roughly 500ms response and ¥0.5 per trial; timing and full cost were not independently checked.
dual-arm-robot-sim.media_note: An approximately 87-second video and three explanatory images form one case; physical deployment is not claimed by this catalog.
dual-arm-robot-sim.review_summary: Layer descriptions and simulation media support a prototype; speed, cost and transfer to hardware remain unverified.

ryze-seo-geo.title: Ryze AI: SEO/GEO audits and fixes
ryze-seo-geo.summary: Add Jev to website visibility audits, analyzing pages and AI-search citations to guide fixes.
ryze-seo-geo.plain_explanation: Like an editor investigating why a site is hard to find: gather pages and citations, judge gaps and arrange edits. New prose still requires a generation stage.
ryze-seo-geo.mechanism: The update details seven judgments in the same product: competitor-page scoring, keep/change decisions for page elements, question-to-page matching, citation-chance scoring, buyer-query classification, screening 15 internal-link candidates and 20 draft checks before human review. Retrieval, writing and execution still require surrounding components.
ryze-seo-geo.advantage: Broader than internal-link suggestions, covering diagnosis and fixes; the broader scope also makes single-model attribution harder.
ryze-seo-geo.limitation: The detail clarifies workflow but does not provide full baseline, quality or billing comparisons. Citation-chance scores are not calibrated citation probabilities or guarantees of rankings/conversions.
ryze-seo-geo.reported_result: The author claims a 90% cost reduction from roughly $250, 30-fold gains across several stages and 20-fold faster page creation. A six-second interface clip does not establish those comparisons.
ryze-seo-geo.media_note: The original clip and new workflow graphic belong to Ryze; reposts of the same performance claims are not separate projects.
ryze-seo-geo.review_summary: Seven additional judgment workflows still belong to one Ryze product. The 90% savings, 20–30-fold speedups and citation effects lack reproducible controls; workflow count does not increase case count.

meeting-flowchart.title: Meeting-to-flowchart: organize a process as people talk
meeting-flowchart.summary: Extract business steps from meeting remarks into an editable flowchart.
meeting-flowchart.plain_explanation: Like a note-taker drawing while listening: decide what matters, ask a language model to organize steps, then check for unsupported or repeated additions.
meeting-flowchart.mechanism: The author describes per-utterance business relevance and add/edit/delete/no-op decisions. Utterances at 50% confidence or above reach an LLM; Jev then checks grounding, duplication and ownership before code updates draw.io.
meeting-flowchart.advantage: Produces an editable draft instead of just scoring interview notes, with separate judgment, writing and diagram stages.
meeting-flowchart.limitation: The 50% cutoff is an author-set threshold, not an accuracy guarantee. Full transcripts, omission rates and human-diagram comparisons are missing.
meeting-flowchart.reported_result: A roughly two-minute fictional real-estate interview is described as normal-speed footage. Low-confidence material is skipped or marked for confirmation.
meeting-flowchart.media_note: Distinct purpose, output and media from this author’s synthetic interview-scoring case.
meeting-flowchart.review_summary: The described workflow and original demo support a prototype, not established accuracy or completeness on complex meetings.

agent-goal-verifier.title: Agent goal verifier: check completion after each turn
agent-goal-verifier.summary: Check whether an agent has actually achieved its goal after every turn.
agent-goal-verifier.plain_explanation: Like a checker beside a task list: the agent acts and Jev judges whether requirements remain unmet.
agent-goal-verifier.mechanism: A custom verifier is integrated into the harness’s /goal feature. Full inputs, criteria and failure handling are not yet public.
